title: Cap. 3 Obj. 9: A-pari — dying for the unsaved as absurd as saving those Christ did not die for
pass_a_gloss: Obj.9 a-pari: dying-for-unsaved as alien as saving those Christ didn't die for — absurd so both false. Sol: deny equal ratio. School: good from complete causes, evil from any defect. Salvation needs full concurrence; loss can follow despite one ordained cause. Impossible to save those Christ didn't die for; not impossible some he died for fall away — God did not decree death alone by offering-fact propitiates/saves all, but placamentum through faith in blood (Rom 3:25) upon all who believe (v.22). Why defend death-as-remedy-for-all but not faith-to-all? Scriptures: dying obtained conditional grace for all/each; that grace couldn't be offered to all unless death belongs to all by ordination. Faith not destined to all — derived from peculiar election. Mediator obtained absolution for believers, willed lytron for all; did not apply merit to all nor obtain infallible faith/salvation for all. Election's secret must not overturn universality of offering / Gospel promise.
pass_b_english: Obj. 9. Some dispute, by an argument drawn from parity, as they think, in this way: It is as far from the truth that Christ by God's ordination died for some who are not saved, as that some are saved for whom by God's ordination he did not die; But this is absurd to say: Therefore that also.

Sol. I deny that the reason is equal on both sides. For (what is most received in the School of Theologians) Good does not arise except from complete causes, evil from any defect whatever. Human salvation, therefore, which is the greatest good, is not produced except by the full concurrence of all causes: but the loss of salvation, which is an evil, once one or another cause ordained to a human being's salvation is in place, can nevertheless occur from the defect of any. Although therefore it is impossible that some human beings be saved for whom Christ did not die, because Christ's death is one of those ordained causes which work human salvation; yet it is not impossible that some for whom he did die fall away from salvation, because it was not established by God that this death of Christ alone by the very fact of offering should render God propitious to all and save all, but that it should be a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the declaring of his righteousness through the remission of sins ([[Romans 3:25 >> Bible:Romans 3:25]]), and so upon all and over all who believe: for there is no distinction, as is had in verse 22. If further someone presses, Why is Christ's death defended as given to all human beings as a remedy, but faith given or prepared for all is not defended? I answer, Because the Scriptures clearly teach that Christ by dying obtained for all and each human being this grace, that under the condition of faith they can now hope for and obtain remission of sins and salvation; but this conditional grace could not be offered to all, nor would it look in any way to all, unless this death of Christ belonged to all human beings by God's own ordination: Now on the other side we do not defend faith as destined or given to all, because the same sacred Scripture which proposes Christ's death as a benefit granted to all, and applicable to anyone through faith, does not make this faith a benefit promised or given to all, but derived from the peculiar decree of election. Add to these that the Mediator himself, who offered himself to God as a sacrifice for expiating the world's sins, obtained from God that all and each who would believe in him should be absolved from sins, and thus far willed to pay this lytron for all: but he did not apply to all the merit of his death, nor obtain from God that all should infallibly follow faith and salvation. And here the secret of election opens, which ought not to overturn or weaken the universality of the offering and the truth of the Gospel promise.
